title: Zak Phase Quantization without Global Symmetry through Destructive Interference
abstract: The Zak phase provides a fundamental geometric characterization of one-dimensional band structures and, when quantized by symmetry, serves as a bulk indicator of polarization and boundary phenomena. Conventionally, its exact quantization is tied to a global symmetry of the Bloch Hamiltonian, such as inversion or reflection symmetry. Here, we demonstrate a distinct mechanism by which the Zak phase remains exactly quantized even when the corresponding protecting symmetry is explicitly broken at the level of the full Hamiltonian. The mechanism is based on local support symmetry and destructive interference: symmetry-breaking degrees of freedom are coupled to a topological parent system in such a way that the relevant Bloch states cannot leak into them. The preserved states therefore retain their parent wave functions and inherit their quantized Zak phase exactly, despite the absence of the protecting global symmetry. We establish this mechanism for general one-dimensional insulators and demonstrate it in an inversion-broken minimal model and a reflection-broken armchair nanoribbon, where a quantized $π$ Zak phase and associated boundary-localized states persist. We further show that perturbations violating the exact destructive-interference condition continuously dequantize the Zak phase, while a finite regime with a near-$π$ Zak phase and boundary response can survive. Our results establish wave-function support, rather than global symmetry alone, as a mechanism for protecting quantized quantum geometry in one-dimensional systems.
summary: This work introduces a novel mechanism showing that the quantized Zak phase in 1D electronic systems can be preserved even when the global symmetry responsible for it is explicitly broken. This protection arises from a 'local support symmetry' condition, which forces the relevant wave functions to remain confined to the parent topological sector via destructive interference. The findings establish wave-function support, rather than global symmetry, as the key guarantor of quantized quantum geometry.
main_problem: To establish a mechanism for the exact quantization of the Zak phase in 1D band structures without relying on a global symmetry of the full Hamiltonian.
main_result: The quantization is protected by a local support symmetry condition, which confines the relevant Bloch states to the parent sector via destructive interference.
method: The analysis uses the construction of an enlarged Hamiltonian by coupling a parent Hamiltonian to a symmetry-breaking sector, and analyzing the resulting eigenstates using projector formalism.
model_or_system: The study focuses on one-dimensional insulators modeled by an enlarged Bloch Hamiltonian $H(k)$ constructed from a parent Hamiltonian $h_A(k)$ and a symmetry-breaking coupling $W(k)$.
key_observables: Zak phase ($\gamma$), which is quantized to $\pi$ in the parent model; the persistence of quantized phase despite symmetry breaking.
important_parameters: The coupling matrix $W(k)$ and the condition $W^\dagger(k)|u_n(k)angle = 0$ (Local Support Symmetry).
main_assumptions: The existence of a parent insulator with a symmetry-quantized Zak phase and the ability to construct a coupling $W(k)$ that enforces the destructive interference condition.
figures_summary: Figures compare bulk and edge spectra for parent models, confirming the presence of the quantized Zak phase ($\gamma_{occ} = \pi$) in both the 'Perfect' and 'Imperfect Pythagorean' cases.
paper_structure: The paper develops the argument by first defining the problem (Zak phase quantization without global symmetry), then introducing the LSS condition via the enlarged Hamiltonian, demonstrating the preservation of the phase, and finally analyzing the failure of the mechanism under perturbation.
why_interesting: The core concept of protecting topological invariants via local wave-function support rather than global symmetries is highly relevant for designing robust quantum devices in condensed matter or photonics.
